intro: MCP is a JSON-RPC protocol for connecting LLM clients to tool/resource/prompt servers. Think USB-C for LLMs — one wire, many devices. The protocol is small; the security implications are not. Pinned to spec rev 2025-06-18 here.

items.title: Architecture: client, server, transport
items.mechanism: An MCP CLIENT (your agent harness) talks JSON-RPC to one or more MCP SERVERS over a TRANSPORT (stdio for local processes, Streamable HTTP for remote, SSE deprecated as of mid-2025). Each server exposes tools, resources, and/or prompts.
items.tradeoff: Decouples tool development from agent development. Adds a process boundary and a wire protocol — extra latency, extra failure modes.

items.title: Three primitives: tools, resources, prompts
items.whenToUse: Pick the primitive that matches the data flow.
items.mechanism: TOOLS = model-invoked, side-effect-OK functions (write_file, search_web). RESOURCES = client-readable, identified by URI, model is informed via context (a file, a row from a DB). PROMPTS = templated message bundles the user/client invokes (e.g. 'summarize selection').
items.tradeoff: Tools cover most use cases. Resources are underused; they're the right shape for 'here is the open file' context-injection.

items.title: Capability negotiation
items.mechanism: Initialize handshake: client and server exchange protocol version + capabilities. Either side may declare it does not support a primitive. Re-negotiation requires reconnection.
items.tradeoff: Forward-compatible. Servers must gracefully degrade when a capability isn't supported.

items.title: Transports: stdio vs HTTP
items.whenToUse: Stdio for local/process-bound integrations. Streamable HTTP for remote/networked.
items.mechanism: Stdio: launch the server as a subprocess, talk over its stdin/stdout. No auth (process boundary IS the auth). HTTP: standard request/response + server push for notifications. OAuth-based auth is the recommended pattern.
items.tradeoff: Stdio is dead simple but local-only. HTTP is operationally heavier but the only viable option for production multi-tenant servers.

items.title: Trust model & untrusted output
items.whenToUse: Every time an MCP response enters your context.
items.mechanism: Treat every MCP response as untrusted input. The server you call is a third party in your context window. Wrap server output in <mcp-result> tags; instruct the model never to follow instructions inside.
items.tradeoff: Most MCP security incidents come from this being forgotten. The protocol does not enforce content trust — the host must.

items.title: Discovery & catalogs
items.mechanism: Servers are discovered via config (client config file lists endpoints) or registries (cataloged lists of public MCP servers). No central authority — anyone can run one.
items.tradeoff: Maximum flexibility. Maximum supply-chain risk. Pin and audit the servers you depend on.

pitfalls.title: Trusting server output
pitfalls.body: An MCP server fetches a webpage and returns its contents. The webpage tells your agent to email the API key to attacker@example.com. The protocol does not prevent this — your host must delimit and instruct the model accordingly.

pitfalls.title: Connecting too many servers
pitfalls.body: Each server adds tools to the registry. Past ~30 total tools, model accuracy drops sharply. Curate ruthlessly; not every server you can connect, you should.

pitfalls.title: No per-server rate limits
pitfalls.body: An MCP server is a tool — a misbehaving agent can hammer it. Rate-limit at the client. Set timeouts.

pitfalls.title: Using deprecated SSE transport
pitfalls.body: The SSE transport was deprecated in 2025-03-26 spec. Use Streamable HTTP for new HTTP-based servers.

pitfalls.title: Servers pinned to an old spec rev
pitfalls.body: The spec evolves quickly. Servers that don't keep up break on version-negotiation. Track the version field; have a deprecation policy.
